articles.title: British comedian and children’s author David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct
articles.summary: Walliams unsuccessfully sought a court injunction to bar news outlets from identifying him, claiming publishing the allegations would lead him to take his own life.
articles.body: LONDON — British children’s author and comedian David Walliams used his fame to groom girls and young women for sex, two British news outlets reported Tuesday. ITV News and The Guardian newspaper said their joint investigation featured interviews with multiple women who gave firsthand accounts of Walliams’ conduct. One woman alleged she was sexually assaulted by Walliams at his London home when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them when they were teens. Walliams, 55, denied the allegations. He unsuccessfully sought a court injunction to bar the news outlets from identifying him, claiming that publication of sexual misconduct allegations would lead him to take his own life. The court fight delayed publication for months, but a judge rejected his injunction request last week, and the protection of his identity expired late Monday. “I am not a sexual predator,” Walliams said in a letter to the news organizations. “I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” “Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did,” he added. Walliams is best known for comedy sketches on “Little Britain,” a hugely popular British TV show in the 2000s, but he’s also a celebrated children’s book author with 40 published titles that sold more than 60 million copies worldwide, according to his website. Several of them, including “Gangsta Granny,” have been adapted into BBC comedy dramas and stage productions. Producers of “Fing!” — an upcoming film based on Walliams’ book — said in a statement Tuesday that they had removed his cameo appearance and that Walliams “will have no involvement in the film’s release or promotion.” He is credited as a co-writer. U.K. distributor Sky told Variety it was dropping the movie. Angel Studios, the U.S. distributor, did not answer The Associated Press’ emailed query about its plans for the film. Walliams was dropped last year by publisher HarperCollins after allegations of inappropriate behavior were made. Few details were published at the time, but the Guardian reported Tuesday that there were concerns about his behavior for years, including an allegation that he had an inappropriate sexual relationship with a junior female employee. He was also a judge for a decade on “Britain’s Got Talent,” though he stepped down in 2022 after apologizing for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants. The BBC said Tuesday it was removing some programs, including “Little Britain,” while it carried out a review of “all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms.” The literary agency Independent Talent Group also said it was dropping Walliams following the new allegations. The court fight, in which Walliams was identified in news reports as a “famous man,” drew widespread attention in Britain because it highlighted questions over public figures’ right to privacy and what media can report on the basis of public interest. Walliams’ lawyer, Sara Mansoori, told the High Court that he had made a suicide attempt when he received letters from ITN and Guardian News and Media seeking his response to the allegations. He later made another attempt, she said, and he was recently admitted to the hospital for psychiatric care. Attorney Gavin Millar, representing the media companies, has said that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a strong public interest in publishing them. Millar told the court that the investigation involved speaking to more than 100 people, and alleged that over a period of years Walliams “used his status and influence as a well-known public figure to establish contact with young women, some considerably younger than him, and that he engaged or sought to engage in seriously inappropriate conduct,” according to a summary of the court judgment. Some of the alleged conduct could amount to criminal offenses if proven, a summary of the court judgment said. The Metropolitan Police in London contacted the news organizations Tuesday to make sure any possible victims knew how to report criminal allegations. In dismissing the injunction bid, Justice Matthew Nicklin said such a legal measure would mean “an exceptionally serious interference” with the rights of the media companies. He noted that Walliams had a “serious and longstanding psychiatric vulnerability” which must be taken seriously, and said a decision allowing the allegations to be published will substantially increase his risk of suicide. However, he added that the evidence did not “establish that suicide is inevitable.”

articles.title: Prince's former manager bought a Los Angeles house for $2.75 million in March, gutted its dated interiors and turned an old dumbwaiter shaft into a lift; now he is asking nearly $5 million
articles.summary: A longtime music executive who helped shape Prince’s career is now betting on a Los Angeles renovation.
articles.body: A longtime music executive who helped shape Prince’s career is now betting on a Los Angeles renovation. Bob Cavallo, the former manager of Prince and a producer associated with Purple Rain, bought a Nichols Canyon house for $2.75 million in March, stripped it back to its essentials, and has listed it for nearly $5 million, according to Mansion Global.The property, built in 1988, had not been meaningfully updated in at least two decades when Cavallo acquired it. Rather than preserve its dated interiors, he and renovation specialist Angie Williams undertook what Williams described as a “total gut,” transforming the house while keeping the character that made it worth saving. Read more details about it, as reported by Mansion Global, here:A home with good bonesThe Nichols Canyon property spans 3,762 square feet and includes four bedrooms. Although it needed extensive work, Cavallo saw potential in its proportions, high ceilings and hillside setting, according to Williams, who oversaw the renovation through her company, House of Renovo.Williams told Mansion Global that the house had “amazing bones” and generous room sizes, but that the interiors were badly in need of modernization. The renovation therefore focused on revealing the home’s strengths rather than turning it into something entirely different.The original Mediterranean design remained the guiding influence. Instead of replacing that identity with a starkly contemporary look, the team incorporated natural materials such as Calacatta marble, oak, Moroccan clay and Venetian plaster.The result is a renovation that feels intentional rather than generic. The house retains its architectural roots, but its finishes, layout and systems have been brought into a more current, polished condition.An elevator from a dumbwaiterOne of the most practical changes involved the home’s vertical layout. Because the house is built into a hillside, its main living areas sit above the garage entrance, creating a challenge for anyone arriving with groceries, luggage or mobility concerns.The renovation team solved that problem by converting an old dumbwaiter shaft into an elevator. The change makes the home easier to navigate while preserving the existing structure and avoiding a more invasive addition.It is the kind of improvement that may not photograph as dramatically as a marble kitchen or a designer bathroom, but it can make a major difference in daily life. In a hillside Los Angeles home, easy movement between levels is not a luxury so much as a functional necessity.The elevator also reflects the broader approach to the renovation. Rather than simply adding square footage or chasing trends, Cavallo and Williams focused on making the existing house work better for modern living.Outside as well as insideThe work was not limited to the interior. The exterior was entirely re-stuccoed, and the roof was replaced, according to Mansion Global. Those are less glamorous improvements than a new kitchen, but they are essential to protecting a home in Los Angeles’s climate and ensuring that the renovation holds up over time.The decision to replace the roof and refresh the exterior also signals that this was not a cosmetic flip. A buyer would be purchasing a home that has been renewed from its structural envelope inward, rather than one that has only received surface-level upgrades.That matters in a market where buyers are increasingly wary of properties that look renovated but still hide aging systems or deferred maintenance. A full exterior refresh, combined with a complete interior overhaul, suggests a more serious investment in the property’s long-term condition.From family purchase to flipCavallo initially bought the Nichols Canyon home for a family member, according to listing agent Angie Williams. When those plans changed, he decided to renovate the property and sell it instead.That shift turned a personal purchase into a real estate project. Cavallo’s background in the music industry may not seem directly related to home renovation, but the same instincts that guide a producer or manager, such as recognizing potential, assembling the right team and knowing when to invest, can translate well into property development.The numbers show the scale of that bet. Cavallo paid $2.75 million in March, then invested in a complete renovation that included new finishes, structural updates, an elevator and exterior work. The home is now listed for just under $5 million.If it sells near that price, the project would represent a substantial gain, though the final profit will depend on the full cost of acquisition, renovation, carrying costs and transaction fees. Mansion Global did not report the renovation budget.Why Nichols Canyon mattersNichols Canyon is a sought-after pocket of the Hollywood Hills, known for its winding streets, hillside homes and proximity to central Los Angeles. Properties there often appeal to buyers who want privacy and views without being far from the city’s studios, restaurants and cultural life.The area’s terrain also shapes its homes. Hillside properties can offer dramatic settings and generous views, but they can require more thoughtful design around access, drainage, parking and movement between levels. Cavallo’s decision to add an elevator speaks directly to that reality.The listing arrives at a moment when Los Angeles luxury real estate remains highly competitive, but also selective. Buyers may be willing to pay a premium for a home that has been thoughtfully renovated, especially when the work addresses both style and function.A renovation with a storyCavallo’s connection to Prince gives the listing a natural hook, but the house itself is the real story. It began as a dated 1988 Mediterranean-style property, was purchased for a family member, then became a full-scale renovation project after those plans changed.By preserving the home’s bones while updating nearly everything else, Cavallo and Williams have created a property that feels both renewed and rooted in its original character. The converted dumbwaiter shaft, in particular, shows how a practical constraint can become an opportunity for smarter design.Now listed for nearly $5 million, the Nichols Canyon house is a test of whether that vision will resonate with buyers. If it does, it will be another example of how a well-executed renovation can turn an overlooked property into one of Los Angeles’s more compelling listings.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? A newly married couple have described the "hilarious" moment when a runaway dog gatecrashed their wedding.

Simon and Amy Keane's wedding was about to begin on Saturday afternoon when a passing Jack Russell sprinted into the church in Eastleigh, Hampshire.

It then ran around members of the congregation and joined the couple's own dog, Duggie, who was due to be a ring bearer.

"I just wanted everything to be perfect," he said. "As all the guests stood up, I thought 'here we go'.

articles.title: Acquitted 'China spy' Chris Cash: I was fall guy for security services but also naive
articles.summary: Thousands of messages seen by BBC show how a Chinese official sought details of sensitive political matters.
articles.body:
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".

Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.

The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.

Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.

The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.

Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.

In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.

But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.

Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.

With the government having previously said that Chinese spies were targeting UK officials across the political, defence and business sectors with increasingly sophisticated espionage operations, Cash believes his case was pursued as a warning to others.

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said he denied any wrongdoing and that he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media".

He said he had provided reports to a Chinese company, which he believed had clients seeking to develop trading links with the UK, and those reports contained no classified information and relied on public sources.

Cash returned to the UK in 2019, saying in his resignation message for his job in China that he felt "guilty sitting back and participating in a system that I am uncomfortable with".

He later became the director of a small policy group run by China-sceptic Conservative MPs in Westminster.

Meanwhile, Berry stayed in China writing reports for a large consultancy which, like many Chinese companies, has links to the government.

UK security services alleged that information from the men's messages, sent on the encrypted messaging app Signal between January 2022 and March 2023, had been passed to people linked to the Chinese state.

England and Wales' top prosecutor said the case had collapsed last autumn because government officials could not say China had been classed as an "enemy" at the time.

This prompted accusations of UK political interference to placate the Chinese government.

China has previously called the allegations of spying "pure fabrication and malicious slander".

The most striking section of the messages handed to the BBC concerns Berry's account of his meeting in summer 2022 with a senior Chinese official who wanted to have "a more detailed co-operation".

In voice notes Berry describes how, beforehand, work colleagues had told him the official's interest had been piqued by reports Berry had written, which included details of the UK's foreign policy approach to China.

In the voice notes, Berry says he was initially aghast, but then decided: "I thought it would be interesting to go anyway… not really intending to do anything."

Berry tells Cash he was driven to a government-owned villa in a grand compound.

The experience "felt like a psychological game of chess" and "like a test", Berry says.

He kept his hands under the table as tea was served: "I didn't want it to be obvious if I was nervous. I tested to see if my hands were shaking first, then drank the tea."

Berry describes the senior Chinese official asking via an interpreter "about the situation in the UK at the moment, about the Tory leadership thing".

At that time, Boris Johnson had just resigned as the UK's prime minister, and a Conservative leadership battle was taking place, which Liz Truss would go on to win.

Berry says he jokingly tried to ask his host which candidate China wanted, but the interpreter did not translate his question.

"And then the main guy just shakes my hand like it's time to go," Berry tells Cash.

After receiving the voice notes, Cash replies via text the next day: "You, my friend, have just been elite captured" before adding: "You're in spy territory now".

In many media reports these particular messages, previously released in a government witness statement, have been presented as a smoking gun - evidence that Cash knew his friend was passing on information to the Chinese state.

But Cash insists it was a "tongue-in-cheek joke" because he knew his friend to be "a staunch critic of the Chinese Communist Party".

The next morning, he made a joke about Berry spying for the UK and getting in trouble with the Chinese authorities, he says. Cash texted: "Keep him sweet… We may have a use for you yet".

"I didn't believe he was knowingly spying on the UK through me," says Cash. "I trusted my friend… I wish I had seen the danger earlier, spotted it and cut off all contact."

So who was the mystery official Berry had met?

"I found out who this guy is," Berry text-messaged Cash a few hours later. "Bigger deal than I thought."

Berry posted a link to the Wikipedia page of Cai Qi, who at the time was one of China's most influential politicians and is now, in effect, President Xi Jinping's chief of staff.

Whether Berry correctly identified his host remains unclear. He has since disputed the suggestion that he met someone as senior as Cai Qi.

What is beyond dispute is that he believed he may have met someone highly placed within the Chinese political system.

For Chris Cash, this unusual encounter did not prompt alarm bells. Asked why not, Cash tells the BBC: "Because I didn't think anything of the meeting, really."

We ask Cash why his friend might have been asked to such a meeting. "Strange things happen in China... you know we would often brush shoulders with sort of quite senior members of the Chinese communist party," he tells us.

Challenged about whether he had read the Wikipedia link at the time, Cash says he had "skimmed it", adding that it described him as a judge and a provincial-level official. "I just thought it was a weird meeting with a guy who'd taken an interest," he says.

Six months later, Berry said in text messages that "off the record" he had it "on pretty good authority" that China was considering dropping sanctions against Tom Tugendhat, one of the Conservative MPs in the China Research Group, where Cash worked.

Berry wrote that this would happen as long as the West "continued to show signals that they are willing to work together".

The Chinese believed it would be "extremely embarrassing" if Tugendhat became prime minister or foreign secretary while under Chinese sanctions, Berry said.

At the time of the meeting in summer 2022, China-sceptic Tugendhat was seen as a possible contender to succeed Boris Johnson, or become UK foreign secretary.

He was actually appointed as security minister by Liz Truss, and Beijing lifted sanctions on him in January 2026.

Was Cash concerned that Berry appeared to be passing information to him about Chinese foreign policy?

Cash says he assumed Berry had heard this "through the grapevine at his company" which was doing business with the UK.

He says he never doubted his friend's trustworthiness, to the extent he even named Berry as a reference on his application for a security pass for the Palace of Westminster.

The pass was granted and, a fortnight before their arrests in early 2023, Cash invited Berry to Parliament for lunch.

It was to be their final face-to-face conversation.

Cash was in bed at quarter to six on a March morning when he was woken by car doors being shut, he says. Within seconds, four UK counter-terrorism officers had barged into his bedroom at his parents' home in Edinburgh.

"They told me to sit up and not touch anything and then said I was under arrest for breaching the Official Secrets Act," Cash says.

"I was in complete shock… quivering... My mum was hysterical."

Cash says the officers dressed him in dirty clothes he had worn that weekend, handcuffed him and marched him down to an unmarked police car. He was later driven to London.

Chris Berry was also arrested the same day.

It remains unclear how, when and why British security services became interested in the exchanges between the two friends.

But they are likely to have found out far more about their relationship when Berry was stopped and questioned by counter-terror officers at Heathrow Airport.

His laptop and phone were taken - this may have enabled his Signal chats to be downloaded.

Cash says he had not been alarmed by this: "I thought it was just standard... for a guy who'd been in China."

As the investigation progressed, it became clear the authorities believed Cash and Berry had been involved in an informal, but dangerous, exchange of information that was "prejudicial to the safety and interests of the UK".

The allegations were based on 6,273 messages between the pair - the same ones Cash has now shared with the BBC. Cash's solicitor has told the BBC they are genuine.

They cover a period when Cash had joined the China Research Group (CRG), founded by Tugendhat and fellow Tory MP Alicia Kearns, and when Berry was working for a Chinese company called Strong, where part of his work involved writing political and economic reports for clients.

According to court documents, Berry was said to have compiled 34 reports for a man linked to the Chinese state spy agency, relaying information passed on to him by Cash. Strong did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

The CRG's office was across the Thames from Westminster, but Cash regularly had meetings in Parliament. Cash did not have government security clearance and there is no evidence he had access to classified documents.

Despite being thousands of miles apart, the two friends remained in close contact, often messaging daily.

The messages reviewed by the BBC show them discussing topics including sanctions on China, the tech company Huawei, human rights, Hong Kong, Taiwan and British foreign policy.

Cash says he used the Signal app for almost all his contacts with people in China - "more for their protection" - as he says discussing the government "could land someone… in trouble". He and Berry did not use the app's "disappearing messages" function.

Much of the information they discussed was publicly available, says Cash - who has given the BBC a detailed spreadsheet with links and references in an attempt to prove it.

But sometimes he did share with Berry his impressions from meetings and private discussions in Westminster. On 12 occasions in the messages, he labelled information "off the record" or "very off the record" before passing it on.

Cash says this was "just me excitedly sharing things that I was doing with him at work".

One message recounted views allegedly expressed in private by Britain's then-ambassador to China, Dame Caroline Wilson, during a discussion with the CRG about its work on China's influence on UK universities.

Cash also messaged Berry sharing unverified rumours about the sex lives of two UK cabinet ministers. There is no evidence Berry passed this to his Chinese colleagues.

Cash says he regarded such exchanges as routine political discussion. "We weren't working with classified information," he says.

Cash was told by his solicitor the police investigation would blow over after six months and he would soon be able to return to normal life.

But in September 2023 - six months after the arrests - the case became public when the Sunday Times broke the story of an unnamed "spy" who had been arrested in Parliament.

Cash recalls travelling on a train while, around him, fellow passengers read the newspaper's front page story: "Commons 'Chinese spy' arrested". He says: "I wanted the world to eat me up."

Within 24 hours he was named and pictured in the press, and both men were later charged with espionage.

In September the following year, just weeks before their trial was due to begin, Cash received an unexpected call from his solicitor.

"Are you sitting down?" he asked Cash. "They've dropped all the charges."

His lawyers requested a court hearing for the prosecution to formally acknowledge that they would offer no evidence, but at the Old Bailey the newly-innocent Cash struggled to find anyone interested in his story.

At every previous court appearance he had been mobbed, but the press had not been informed about this hearing.

Eventually his team found a lone BBC journalist. "I said my piece outside the Old Bailey. And that was a real high point. I felt that I could start to move on with my life."

Across the city, House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle was seething. "It is this Parliament that has been spied on," he declared. "It is MPs' offices that have been infiltrated."

There would be days of political debate and a raucous prime minister's questions where Tory leader Kemi Badenoch would claim: "This all stinks of a cover-up."

"I'd been acquitted by law, but then I was traduced in Parliament," Cash says. "It was almost like I was convicted in the court of public opinion again, by people who I had worked with and trusted and that felt horrible."

Today Cash's life is almost unrecognisable. He has lost his dream job, his relationship, and his closest friend from university.

"We talked about being each other's best men," Cash says. Instead, when the friend got married last year, Cash was not even invited.

He is also no longer in contact with Berry.

"I've been applying for basic admin jobs and having trouble recently," Cash says.

"I'm angry and upset with how everything played out, and I do feel let down."

But when asked, Cash stops short of saying he feels Berry betrayed him. Does he think his friend was spying for the Chinese government?

"He would have to have his time in court to defend himself," Cash answers. "I think it'd be wrong of me to speculate and hypocritical given the speculation that I've been subject to. But we're no longer friends."

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said his reports "concerned economic and commercial issues widely discussed in the UK at the time and drew on information freely in the public domain".

Like his former friend, Chris Cash is innocent in the eyes of the law, but his reputation has undoubtedly been trashed.

Many in Parliament still think they were spies. And with more of the messages between these former friends now revealed, the debate over their actions could be reignited.

"It was a gruelling ordeal," Cash says. "But I'm a fundamentally positive person… I'm positive about what the future holds."

articles.title: Sleaford waste centre near homes approved despite local concern
articles.summary: The facility would be close to Sleaford's Holdingham Grange housing development.
articles.body:
A waste processing facility in a Lincolnshire town has been approved despite concerns it is too close to local housing.

Clean Planet Energy has been granted permission to build a waste plastic processing plant on land at Sleaford Moor Enterprise Park.

Speaking at a meeting on Monday, Councillor Steve Clegg said he did not believe there had been "meaningful community engagement" with people living on the nearby Holdingham Grange housing development.

However, planning officers said the application had followed the required consultation process and people had sufficient opportunities to raise their concerns.

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , the site will process up to 25,000 tonnes of previously non-recyclable plastic waste per year – which would otherwise have been sent to landfill, incinerated or polluted the environment.

The plastic will be turned into reusable energy products and fuels.

The development will operate 24 hours a day, generating up to 76 two-way lorry movements per week.

At the meeting, Clegg said: "Many residents moved to Holdingham Grange expecting light industrial business use at Sleaford Moor Enterprise park.

"They are now being asked to accept a plastics and chemical processing facility just a few hundred metres from their homes."

However, members decided to approve the application, with Councillor Matthew Boles saying he was "struggling to find any planning reasons" to refuse it.

Representing Clean Planet Energy, agent Robert Doughty said the facility was on land allocated for commercial development and the company would employ more than 30 staff at the site.

He added: "We're aware of the proximity to residential development, particularly looking at Holdingham Grange to the west, where the nearest house is around 350 metres (383 yards) from the application site."

Doughty said officer reports had concluded the plant would not have a "detrimental impact" on the area.

articles.title: Greta Thunberg blasts UN climate talks as ‘hypocrisy’ at COP31
articles.summary: Climate activist Greta Thunberg arrived at U.N. climate talks on Tuesday, condemning the annual proceedings as hypocritical and urging leaders to put people and the planet ahead of profits and power.
articles.body: ANTALYA, Turkey — Climate activist Greta Thunberg arrived at U.N. climate talks on Tuesday, condemning the annual proceedings as hypocritical and urging leaders to put people and the planet ahead of profits and power. The COP31 conference is being held in the Turkish resort city of Antalya following a year of deadly climate-related disasters, including heat waves and floods, and another energy shock caused by the Iran war. “It’s a hypocrisy every year that the host countries are given an opportunity to whitewash themselves and we know that these negotiations are filled with lobbyists, paid by the very destructive industries which are benefiting from our extremely violent status quo,” Thunberg said as she arrived. “Our political and economic systems that have become incompatible with human nature.” COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia are promoting renewable energy and rooftop solar installations, but both still rely heavily on fossil fuels, especially coal, to generate electricity. Previous hosts, including Brazil, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan, are major oil producers. Climate change is “threatening everything,” Thunberg said, warning that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.” “We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she said. Thunberg blasts annual talks This is the first climate summit Thunberg has attended since the 2021 talks in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed world leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah.” She rose to prominence in 2018 when, aged 15, she began a solitary “ School Strike for Climate “ outside the Swedish Parliament. In 2022, she published “The Climate Book,” outlining actions to address the climate crisis. She has won multiple awards and advocated for other causes, including the Free Palestine movement. Last year, she was arrested in London while supporting hunger-striking pro-Palestinian activists. More recently, she supported French students protesting for more school resources. In 2024, she joined a protest in Georgia against Azerbaijan’s hosting of COP29. A key goal for Turkey is global electrification: shifting sectors such as transportation, buildings and heavy industry away from fossil fuels and toward electricity. Turkey wants electricity, preferably generated from renewable sources such as solar and wind, to account for 35% of global energy consumption by 2035, up from 23% today. “We have to take the victories we have, of course, because we are so desperate in this situation that we have to take all the positive signs we can get to save as much as we can still save,” said Thunberg, who is expected to spend several days at COP31. Youth activists rally Thunberg’s arrival at the conference created excitement among many youth climate activists. “In this time of heightened geopolitical tensions, I hope that Greta’s presence here reminds us of why we started this work in the first place: to push for meaningful change, hold decision-makers accountable, and work towards a better future for all of humanity,” said Amber Turner, a 26-year-old fellow with the Alliance of Small Island States. “Worsening climate change impacts make it challenging for young people to be sure of a safe and thriving future,” Turner added. Protests at COP31 demanded more climate finance and criticized growing interest in nuclear energy. “The presence of such a headline climate activist at one of the world’s biggest conferences on climate is symbolic, and I hope that it will put pressure on the COP itself to deliver real action and implementation,” said Kamori Osthananda, a youth negotiator with Thailand’s COP delegation. Qiyun Woo, a youth environmentalist from Singapore, said Thunberg’s “powerful” presence “adds to calls from a generation that inherits the consequences of these negotiations.” “Besides her, there are many youth activists from around the world who are also on the ground who are actively fighting for their communities, home and collective future,” she said. The U.N. talks in Antalya run until Nov. 20. COP32 is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

articles.title: 'Winter extravaganza' planned after Big Burns Supper's demise
articles.summary: The festival brought some big names to Dumfries but a new "winter extravaganza" is taking its place.
articles.body:
Plans for a three-day "winter extravaganza" in Dumfries have been unveiled following the demise of the Big Burns Supper (BBS) festival.

Organisers admitted the old format - which brought big name artists to the town for more than a decade - was "never really sustainable".

In its place is an entirely free Dumfries and Galloway Carnival programme from 29 to 31 January with light installations, music and hundreds of community performers.

Executive producer Graham Main said they were aware money was tight for many people and he hoped the new format was right for the town and the region as a whole.

Last Supper: Why the Burns festival in Dumfries has called it a day

Out of this world: Dumfries carnival goes intergalactic

The first BBS took place in 2012 and was made up of 80 events covering music, dance, comedy, theatre and art across 40 different venues.

Acts ranging from Nina Nesbitt to the Undertones and Black Grape to the Bay City Rollers would come to perform and, within a few years, it was a nine-day event.

However, after the Covid pandemic, it struggled to recover and was cancelled in 2024 after it failed to secure funding from EventScotland.

It returned but organisers confirmed earlier this year that it was the end of the road for the festival in the format that brought the Spiegeltent venue to town.

Main told BBC Scotland News: "It never really was sustainable, if I'm being perfectly honest.

"Even up until the pandemic, whilst the public might have experienced world class culture, we were very honest about the fact that it never quite broke even."

He said they had learned during Covid to "think outside the box" and he believed they had done so again with their new plans.

"I think what we have always been very good at is trying to tune into what feels right for right now," he said.

"And we are taking a temperature reading and we don't think people have got that much money after Christmas.

"So, therefore, actually what's more important to us is bringing people back together to connect."

Main said they hoped to bring the same "magical energy" as before - just presented in a different way.

"I think what we've done is we've sort of used the abundant resources which we have - which is empty shops and derelict buildings on our High Street," he added.

"I think we've tried to turn that into a positive because what we've done with Northern Lights is really utilise those empty spaces."

The event includes three days of live music, a winter village in the town centre and street traders.

A parade - which attracted thousands of people this year - will return in 2027 with lanterns being made across the south west of Scotland

"There are few times we actually come together as a region, even in football, you know, we're split between various towns," said Main.

"So it's nice to have a reason to be called one Dumfries and Galloway, isn't it?"

articles.title: Filmmakers in push to make Jersey a screen destination
articles.summary: Filmmakers are calling for a screen commission to help attract more productions to Jersey.
articles.body:
The film industry is calling for the creation of a new commission to make it easier for productions to shoot in Jersey.

Filmmakers, politicians and investors met at the Jersey Screen Summit on Monday to discuss developing a sustainable film and television industry.

It was organised by director Rebecca Coley as a way to get government and film sector representatives "on the same page" and she said the creation of a commission would "be a one port of call for all productions happening here".

Assistant Economic Development Minister Senator Serena Kirsten said the government was looking at options to support the industry but added further talks were needed to get it "right".

Coley said a film commission could help producers deal with the island's layers of governments including the parish system.

"They could liaise with all the different departments because it is quite confusing as an outsider understanding all our parishes and who to speak to for all the different elements that you need for filming," she said.

"That's what they have in most other places in the world where filming takes place, one central office takes care of all the permits and deals with all the different departments to help make it smooth sailing while the production happens."

She acknowledged that one of the biggest barriers to attracting productions was the cost of filming on island.

"All the other jurisdictions where filmmaking takes place have incentives like a cash rebate or a tax incentive ," she said.

"At the moment, because Jersey doesn't have any of those things that's why we haven't seen more productions here.

"I think because Jersey needs to diversify its economy, let's give this a chance."

Brian Constantine, executive producer of the reboot of the TV show Bergerac, said the series had shown what was possible in terms of developing the industry.

While parts of the series are filmed in Jersey, filming has also taken place in the UK.

"There are inherently much larger costs coming to Jersey at the moment. For example we're putting up a hundred people every time we come here - that's a huge amount of the budget that we wouldn't necessarily be spending if we were using UK crews."

He said creating a film commission would be a "one stop shop" for anyone wanting to film the island.

"They'll be able to tell you what you can do, what you can't do, all the things that you don't think about when you're watching a TV show," he said.

"We've been able to demonstrate that we can make a television show that sells around the world in little old Jersey and Jersey can compete in the right environment on that world stage."

Samantha Perahia, head of production at the British Film Commission, said Jersey already had the building blocks of a successful industry.

She said the island had an "abundance" of locations but she added cast, crew and facilities were needed to support production.

"You also need some kind of incentive in order to be able to compete with other jurisdictions that maybe have similar offers," she said.

"[Having] a central point of contact and a relationship between industry and government like a film commission gives that seed to build on.

"There has to be some demonstrable value, both to the industry, to the local economy, but also to the filmmakers."

The summit heard how developing the industry could give young people the chance to follow careers in film without leaving Jersey.

Finley Lumsden, who worked as a trainee on Bergerac for three seasons, said it was hard to pursue a career in film "because there isn't that much [in Jersey]".

"With these big productions and incentives that the island will hopefully produce, it means more things can happen and more local people can be hired and trained," he said.

The assistant economic development minister said the sector had "potential and real promise".

Senator Kirsten said: "Where I'd like to go next with all of this is just to continue on some of the positive things that were mentioned around tax incentives in the film industry in Jersey and actually trying to get an understanding about what it means for us as an island.

"I would hate to introduce a new sector into the island and not get it right from an incentive perspective because from what I've heard that's pretty important in terms of attracting the diversification that the film industry offers."

articles.title: Netanyahu fights to stay relevant as Israel’s opposition closes in
articles.summary: A new Knesset shaped by October 7 prepares to convene as Netanyahu fights to prevent an opposition-led government
articles.body:
In the last few days, in marked contrast to an election campaign defined by its bitterness and the closeness of its personal attacks, Israel’s current prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken of national unity and coming together with the opposition bloc that edged out his ruling coalition in October’s election.

On Saturday, the same day that Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government capable of commanding the Knesset, Netanyahu published a video on his social media account claiming Israel to be facing the genuine risk of civil war i f a government were established with the support of Arab parties which he accused of wanting to “eliminate the State of Israel”.

Two days later, Netanyahu returned to the theme of existential threat in a further video, calling upon the leaders of the more successful bloc to recognise the “needs of the hour” and join, under his leadership, a single unified government that would also include the ultra-Orthodox parties, at least one of which is understood to be in talks with Eisenkot, as well as the prime minister’s controversial allies on the far right, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir.

“It’s all a game at the moment. It’s leverage, it’s one-upmanship, it’s psyops, it’s spin, it’s counter-spin,” former Israeli government adviser Daniel Levy said of the invariably long and complex negotiations that take place ahead of establishing a government

Currently, with the new Knesset being sworn in on Tuesday, speculation is focussing on the role of the Ultra Orthodox, or haredim, parties, which have traditionally offered support to Netanyahu in return for measures shielding their young male yeshiva students from the military draft in defiance off a Super Court ruling of June 2024 .

Nevertheless, irrespective of the past political cover offered to their members by Netanyahu, there are suggestions that one of the Ultra Orthodox parties United Torah Judaism (UTJ) – which refused to endorse Netanyahu’s selection to build a government by the President – is preparing to throw in behind Eisenkot, with the objections of one of the opposition’s principal figures Avigdor Lieberman said to be quieted in the face of either partnering with one of the Arab parties or the continued rule of Lieberman’s nemesis, Netanyahu and the prospect of further elections.

“‘It’s political strategy, that’s all,” Netanyahu’s former aide, Israeli pollster Mitchell Barak said from Jerusalem. ‘But he’s negotiating from a weakened position. With the UTJ, Eisenkot’s got 67 seats,’ he said of the numbers needed to gain a working majority in the 120 seat Knesset, “so, of course, Netanyahu’s going to do all he can to reinforce his bloc; Barak said of negotiations regarded by many as critical to Netanyahu’s personal future.

Netanyahu faces a number of challenges that speak directly to both his political legacy and personal freedom that he will lose all influence over should Eisenkot succeed him.

Foremost are like to be the multiple corruption charges that is is presently on trial for and, despite his claims of innocence that he has already preemptively petitioned the country’s President and his former political rival, Isaac Herzog for. Secondly, and more pressingly is the question of his and his government’s culpability for the alleged failings ahead of the October 7 Hamas led attack that triggered the genocide unleashed upon Gaza by Israel and the multiple strikes and attacks launched by Israel non regional neighbors in the years since.

Many of the new MKs being sworn in on Tuesday, including bereaved family members, reservists, advocates for the 250 or so Israelis taken captive that day and Eisenkot himself, who lost a son and two nephews in the genocide that followed, are all tied directly to October 7 and the wars that followed together creating a chamber where feelings over the October 7 attack and where culpability for its lies are said to run close to the surface.

In particular, attention is likely to focus sharply on Netanyahu himself, whose supposed miscalculations ahead of the attack, stories of numerous missed warnings and who was subsequently accused of dragging out the war, or sacrificing the welfare off the captives for his own political ends. Key among the opposition’s aims for the first day of parliamentary business is set to be the installation of Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar (“straight”) party and a keen advocate of a state inquiry into Netanyahu and the government’s failings ahead of the Hamas led attack.

“Having so many people connected so directly to October 7 is going to increase the temperature, but it’s become so politicized that a win for one side automatically becomes a loss for the other, so the bereaved family on the right can say we need to increase our militarism in honor of my son, and the bereaved family in the center says we need to enlist more people.

“Netanyahu can try to influence that but for the first time in a long time, he seems a bit lost,” Israeli political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg said.

However, how lost Netanyahu may be, or how grounded his claims of pending civil war or destruction at the hands of regional adversaries may be, ultimately, his political and potentially personal fate now lies with an opposition that outstrips his own numerically and a volatile Knesset eager to comb over the mistakes of the past.

“There’s no appetite on the other side to go in with Netanyahu for a unity government,” Levy said

“The only real circumstances under which that happen is if he can create a security emergency,” he said following a weekend where the UK press had reported daily phone calls from Netanyahu to the Trump administration urging renewed war on Iran.

articles.title: Chumbawamba star writes new 'Anthem for Burnley'
articles.summary: Boff Whalley, a founding member of the Burnley band, wrote the song for the town's Year of Culture 2027.
articles.body:
A musician behind one of the biggest British hits of the 1990s has written a new anthem for Burnley's Year of Culture 2027 celebrations.

Boff Whalley, a founding member of Burnley-based Chumbawamba, wrote and produced Ours to Make with the aim of capturing the spirit of the Lancashire town.

People in the town will get their first chance to hear the track when it is performed live during the Burnley Believes stage show on St James's Street on Saturday.

Burnley's Year of Culture aims to celebrate the borough's creativity, heritage and communities through a programme of events designed to boost civic pride, support local artists and attract visitors and investment.

Whalley, whose band enjoyed worldwide success with their 1997 hit Tubthumping, said one of the strengths of the Year of Culture project was its focus on participation.

"It's not just going 'Here's a showcase of people who've done things'," he said.

"It gives you the inspiration or the incentive to think 'I want to get involved, I could do something like that'."

Describing Ours to Make as a Northern Soul-inspired track, Whalley said he hoped it would bring people together.

"The barometer of success for this song so far is having people on the street joining in and having a dance to it," he said.

Preparations for Burnley 2027 have continued to gather momentum, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said, with a report for the Burnley Town Board revealing that more than £1.1m had already been secured for the programme.

Organisers including the borough council are also seeking a further £350,000 from the government's Pride in Place Fund.

Whalley explained that conversations with local residents had influenced the song's message.

Rather than focusing solely on Burnley's industrial past, he said people had urged him to reflect the town's modern identity, resilience and future potential.

"I think I got involved because I had the good fortune of being born within two miles of Turf Moor," he said. "It was calling me."

He added that residents had told him: "Don't make it all about cotton", prompting him to focus instead on Burnley's enduring spirit of industry and ambition for the future.

articles.title: Russell Brand's £3k donation to Grays victims' charity after rape
articles.summary: A rape crisis centre says it received a donation in the disgraced entertainer's name in 2010.
articles.body:
Russell Brand made a donation to a rape crisis charity in his hometown a year after committing the offence himself, it has emerged.

The donation of £3,000 was given to South Essex Rape and Incest Crisis Centre (SERICC) in the disgraced entertainer's name, to help pay for its 25th anniversary party.

The charity, based at Grays, in Thurrock, Essex, received the money in late 2010. Brand has since been convicted of raping a 21-year-old woman in 2009.

SERICC founder Sheila Coates said: "He supported four or five local charities in the area he was from, but this is really about his abuse of power, the other part of the Russell Brand personality."

The charity had no dealings with Brand directly but received the donation from his management team to help pay for a party at a venue called Orsett Hall in December 2010.

Coates added: "We were engaged in fundraising activity and wrote to lots of famous people and asked for a donation and he happened to be on the list.

"We were responded to by his management, not him, he wasn't in the country. We had no contact with him at all."

Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault

Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand

Brand was born and brought up in the area, attending Grays School, now known as the Hathaway Academy.

In 2013, he opened the Thurrock Mind charity shop in Grays.

In 2022, he campaigned to save the Thameside Theatre over concerns it would be sold off by cash-strapped Thurrock Council.

Coates said: "There is something about celebrity, money, power, control. When you get fame and money, some men abuse that position and that's what he's done.

"We've seen this so many times with famous men, it's not a shock it's disappointment and it goes on and on and on, that's the disappointment, not really the shock because we've seen this with others."

Brand is now serving a sentence of 10 years and six months after being found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Coates believed there would be "positives and negatives" after the high-profile case when it came to other victims of sexual assault coming forward.

She was concerned about "victim blaming" since the outcome, adding: "I've heard things like 'it was a long time ago', 'why didn't she report it sooner?'.

"That's all normal behaviour for victims for all sorts of logical psychological reasons.

"We still need to do some work around the myths and facts around sexual assault, all judges are supposed to do that, but I don't think all of them do, so we've got to make sure that happens so that justice is fair and victims are not blamed for their own assault."

articles.title: Giant mural brings Stoke-on-Trent's clubbing past to life
articles.summary: Artist Tom Edwards is starting work on a large mural to celebrate the city's clubbing heritage.
articles.body:
Work has begun on a large mural celebrating Stoke-on-Trent's clubbing heritage.

Two former DJs, Phil Johnson and Bob Leigh, wanted to pay tribute to the city's venues and its DJs and raised £11,000 needed for the project.

Local artist Tom Edwards, who has been tasked with creating the work, said it had been a difficult process finalising the design, as there had been so many suggestions of stories and themes from the large community the pair had created.

The artwork is being painted onto the side of a bar on Adventure Place, Hanley, and he is aiming to complete it by mid-December.

It nods to a range of local clubs from across the decades, including The Golden Torch , The Place , The Void and Maxims, as well as DJs like Keith Minshull, Trevor M, Dave Evison and Pete Bromley .

In 2025, Leigh and Johnson installed blue plaques at sites where historic venues and nightclubs once stood.

Leigh said the "tremendous response" to the plaques inspired the mural. They announced plans for the 5m (16ft) by 25m (82ft) artwork in January.

The initial plan was to produce a series of small paintings to go next to the plaques. Instead, they decided "to go big or go home," Leigh said.

"It's been a long time coming, this has, for various reasons, and the past few months have been very fraught. But we've got Tom, so we're winning."

Edwards' work can already be seen across the city. He is best known for wildlife murals, the most recent of which is on the Trent and Mersey Canal near Stoke railway station.

articles.title: Ernie and Merrillyn Cole have recorded rainfall from the same Australian home since 1963; now aged 86 and 82, they want an automatic weather station so the 63-year record can continue as they travel
articles.summary: For more than six decades, Ernie and Merrillyn Cole have made looking at the skies part of their daily routine.
articles.body: For more than six decades, Ernie and Merrillyn Cole have made looking at the skies part of their daily routine. From their home in Victoria's Mitta Mitta Valley, the Australian couple have diligently monitored local weather conditions, preserving a record that has become an important resource for the region. At 86 and 82, they want to pass the baton to technology so they can travel and continue their incredible weather recording legacy.As reported by ABC News and Lifestyle News, the couple are appealing to Australia's Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) to install an automatic weather station at their property, replacing the manual observations they have maintained since 1963.A family routine that became a lifelong commitmentThe Coles arrived in the Mitta Mitta Valley in north-east Victoria in 1963, when Ernie was employed as a forestry officer with the state government. Part of his responsibilities involved reporting local weather conditions to the BOM using an observation station situated outside their home.However, with early starts required for his work, Merrillyn gradually took over the daily task. The responsibility became part of family life, with her often making the journey to the weather station while looking after their young children.What started as a practical arrangement became a 63-year commitment.The couple sends rainfall data from the same property, continuing a regional weather record from before their time.According to ABC News, Ernie also inherited historical observations from Mitta Mitta's former postmistress when he assumed responsibility for the station. Since the town's weather records date to 1915, their data will be archived.Why maintaining the same location mattersFor Ernie, the value of the observations lies not just in their longevity but also in their consistency. He believes measurements must continue from precisely the same location to ensure that future readings remain comparable with historical data.This is particularly important in the Mitta Mitta Valley, where rainfall patterns can differ considerably over relatively short distances.Their neighbour and friend Russell, known locally as Ned Kelly, has also supported the campaign for an automatic weather station. A retired pilot who operates the local airfield, Kelly is familiar with the area's distinctive microclimate and understands the importance of reliable weather information.As highlighted by ABC News and Lifestyle News, rainfall can vary significantly even between locations separated by just 10 kilometres, with differences of approximately 300 millimetres recorded across the valley.Kelly has also raised concerns about a gradual decline in rainfall over the past century, arguing that consistent local observations are essential for farmers trying to understand changing conditions and plan agricultural activities.A technology-led solution for a 63-year legacyThe Coles are not looking to abandon their contribution to the community. Instead, they want an automated system that can preserve the accuracy of their observations without requiring their daily presence.Over the years, the BOM's reporting requirements have also evolved. Merrillyn previously received daily telephone calls to report temperature, wind conditions, frost and fog. However, approximately a year ago, the bureau informed her that routine rainfall calls were no longer necessary unless there was particularly heavy precipitation.Australia's weather-monitoring network has increasingly embraced automation. The BOM operates more than 650 automatic weather stations nationwide, while approximately 3,000 manual observation sites continue to function. Automated technology has progressively replaced many traditional stations since the 1980s.However, the bureau has not confirmed whether it intends to install a new station at the Coles' property. According to its response reported by ABC News, there are already two automatic weather stations approximately 39 kilometres away and another automated rain gauge six kilometres from Mitta Mitta. It also indicated that volunteer rainfall observations in the town would continue, with no immediate plans to discontinue them.Time for a well-earned holidayUntil a permanent solution emerges, the couple intend to continue recording rainfall for as long as they are physically able. When they travel, Kelly steps in to maintain the observations, having even postponed holidays previously to ensure the records are not interrupted.A couple could leave home without cover with an automatic station, allowing them to explore while maintaining data continuity.Lifestyle News and ABC News recounted their experience, highlighting regional volunteer weather observers' unsung work. Behind the forecasts and figures accessed through everyday weather applications are individuals who have dedicated years to documenting changing environmental conditions.For the Coles, a new automatic weather station would mean more than a technological upgrade. It would ensure that a record begun in 1915, carefully maintained through generations, continues from the very same spot, while finally giving its longest-serving observers the freedom to take a holiday.Images Courtesy: ABC Rural/Annie Brown and istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: UK weather: Temperatures to dip to -5C as cold health alerts issued
articles.summary: The most widespread frost of the season so far is forecast for many parts of the country. BBC Weather's Tomasz Schafernaker reports.
articles.body:
The first cold health alerts of the season have been issued for parts of England as a blast of Arctic air is set to sweep into the UK.

From midweek onward, overnight temperatures in many towns and cities will fall below zero, bringing the most widespread frost of the season so far.

Some rural spots could see overnight temperatures as low as minus 5C or lower.

Sleet and snow will be possible in some far northern locations with strong wind gusts causing bitter conditions.

First cold health alerts of season issued

Yellow cold health alerts, issued by UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), cover the West Midlands and the north west of England. , external

They will be in place from 09:00 GMT on Thursday until 12:00 GMT on Saturday.

Cold health alerts are usually issued between 1 November and 30 March.

The UKHSA warns the upcoming cold snap "is likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services" and pose "greater risk to life of vulnerable people".

How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips

Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed

What does an unheated room do to your body?

After the thick fog of recent days , visibility will be better on Wednesday, with crisp sunshine forecast for many parts of the UK.

Low pressure and a weather front will graze southern parts of Britain, bringing outbreaks of rain and slightly milder air with highs reaching 10 to 14C.

Late on Wednesday, cloud will clear ahead of Arctic air surging southwards across the country.

By Wednesday night, a strong to gale force northerly wind will develop over northern and eastern parts of Scotland making it feel especially bitter with gusts exceeding 50mph.

Showers are expected to stream in with sleet and snow possible in Shetland and Orkney as well as northern Scotland.

Over higher ground, snow may settle into Wednesday night. This is not unusual for early November.

Winds will also strengthen along the North Sea coast all the way down to the coast of Norfolk making it feel very cold .

Winds will remain strong on Thursday across the far north of the UK. However, inland it will be calm as a ridge of high pressure builds.

Widespread frost is expected across the northern half of the UK while the southern half holds on to the somewhat milder morning conditions for a little while longer.

Thursday afternoon is expected to be sunny across much of the country though showers, some of which could be wintry, may still continue in the far north.

While Thursday morning may feel cold across much of the country, daytime highs will still typically reach 7C.

The northerly breeze will make it feel colder in some places.

On Thursday evening, the weather will be clear and calm across much of the country as temperatures fall rapidly.

Winds will have eased somewhat across Northern Scotland and along the North Sea coast.

Friday will bring frost on grass, pavements and cars in many parts as the air temperature falls below zero from Scotland to Southern England.

Most towns and cities will experience temperatures around zero or just below, while rural spots in Scotland and even southern England chill to minus 5C.

Counties along western and southern western coasts of the UK will not be quite as cold, as the warmer sea and an onshore breeze will prevent frost from forming.

Inland, after a frosty morning, daytime highs will peak at 6 or 7C for most.

Saturday and Sunday night will be cold and frosty in some southern and eastern parts of the country.

By the weekend though, milder weather will already be spreading in from the Atlantic making the cold snap rather brief for most.

articles.title: Is Washington rethinking its relationship with Israel?
articles.summary: The midterms exposed a growing challenge to decades of US support for Israel, with potentially lasting consequences.
articles.body:
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu eventually leaves office – and he may be on his way out sooner rather than later, following last month’s general election – he will leave behind a long record of damage inflicted on his country and its people, as well as on others.

Strategically, however, one of his most damaging legacies, particularly for the security and wellbeing of the Jewish state, will be the rapid deterioration of its relations with its closest and most consequential ally, the United States. This is not simply a falling-out with America’s political elite; relations with the American public have also suffered.

Worse still, replacing Netanyahu may not be enough to halt the erosion of relations between the two countries, with potentially serious consequences for Israel’s security, economy and international standing. A change of government might, at best, salvage some of what has been lost.

US President Donald Trump’s announcement, on the day of the US midterm elections, that the United States would phase out approximately $4bn in annual military aid to Israel by the end of 2026 came as a surprise, primarily because of its timing and the prospect that decades of assistance would come to such an abrupt end.

It may have been a last-ditch attempt to avert a landslide Congressional victory for the Democrats, but the decision to gradually phase out the aid had reportedly been agreed some time earlier.

Nevertheless, the direction of travel in US-Israeli relations is clear: the almost automatic and unwavering support extended by successive US administrations, particularly since 1967, is cooling. There have, of course, been occasional exceptions, but Washington has generally supported Israel even when the policies and actions of its government have not necessarily served American national interests.

There are both long-term trends and more immediate reasons behind this changing attitude in Washington and among the wider American public, the latter including Israel’s conduct under Netanyahu’s sixth government, the most far-right in the country’s history.

For some, Israel’s actions have drawn the US into conflicts that have damaged its international reputation, placed close American allies in the region in harm’s way and proved extremely costly financially.

For many on the progressive-liberal side of the political spectrum, the principal concerns have been the disproportionate use of deadly force by Israel in its war in Gaza; the brutal and ruthless occupation of the Palestinian Occupied Territories (OPT); and the continued expansion of settlements, with the clear and deeply troubling intention of annexing at least the West Bank, if not the Gaza Strip too.

Contrary to what the Israeli government often suggests, the vast majority of these critics are neither anti-Israel nor anti-Semitic.

However, they find it difficult to accept that American money and weapons have been used in the destruction of Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of innocent Palestinians, who had nothing to do with Hamas’s massacre on October 7, 2023. Nor can they accept the terrorist violence perpetrated by extremist settlers against Palestinians, often with complete impunity. Such actions run counter to the very core of their values, as they should to those of anyone with even a shred of humanity.

For the America First MAGA movement, the narrative that Israel dragged the US into a war that failed to achieve its objectives, cost the American military $47bn according to US military’s own estimates, and contributed to a sharp increase in the cost of living may be exaggerated. Nevertheless, the underlying desire to cut military aid to Israel, as well as to other countries, is genuine.

Ironically, one of the few areas where the MAGA movement and the more radical progressive-liberal camp converge is their opposition to spending billions of dollars on foreign military assistance when that money could instead be directed towards pressing domestic needs.

There is, of course, an element of populism in this argument. Addressing America’s healthcare crisis, homelessness and youth unemployment, among other problems, would require considerably more than the approximately $4 billion in annual aid Israel receives. Nevertheless, if that assistance is also seen as harming American interests, those who hold this view see little reason to continue supporting it.

Vice President JD Vance’s attempt, following the Republicans’ poor performance in the midterm elections, to place the principal responsibility for the deterioration of relations on Israel smacks of a cynical attempt to deflect blame and evade responsibility. The world’s most powerful country has its own intelligence community. It should not rely exclusively on Israeli assessments before going to war, particularly when deciding whether to heed Israeli encouragement to confront Iran. If Washington did rely on Netanyahu’s assessment, which subsequently proved misleading, whether deliberately or otherwise, that the war would be short, lead to regime change and result in the complete elimination of Iran’s nuclear programme, then responsibility must also rest with the US administration.

Nevertheless, the relationship between the US and Israel is fundamentally asymmetric. Israel obtains nearly 70 percent of its imported major arms from the US, relies on American diplomatic support in the international arena and is also an important trading partner. Washington can therefore afford, far more than Israel, to reconsider the exceptional status Israel has enjoyed in shaping American regional policies and relations with international organisations.

This is not to suggest that the close relationship between the US and Israel is about to break down completely. However, it is bound to change, driven by both geopolitical and geoeconomic considerations. Moreover, politicians, particularly with another presidential election only two years away, can increasingly sense the electorate’s changing mood. Many are therefore likely to distance themselves from an excessively close relationship with Israel and make continued support more conditional on a demonstrable convergence of interests.

To understand the significance of this shift, it is worth recalling that American support for Israel has traditionally rested on three principal pillars.

The first was sympathy following the Holocaust, together with recognition of the need for a Jewish state as a safe haven for those who had suffered persecution and for future generations.

The second was the perception that the two countries shared liberal-democratic values.

The third was Israel’s emergence as a strong and independent military ally in an unstable region, capable of relying on its own military personnel and capabilities, while benefiting from American military hardware and assistance.

With the collective memory of the horrific fate of European Jewry during the Second World War gradually fading, the first pillar is weakening.

Israel’s democratic credentials are increasingly under scrutiny at home, and its democratic values are absent from its treatment of Palestinians in the OPT; the second pillar is also under strain.

Meanwhile, the war with Iran and the conflicts on other fronts have raised questions about whether Israel is ultimately more of an asset or a burden to American interests. The midterm elections have brought these tensions to a head and may foreshadow where US-Israeli relations are heading.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Chinese university buys Nvidia AI H200 chips despite US ban, records show
articles.summary: Investigation reveals Chinese entities accessing US-restricted AI tech despite stringent export control measures.
articles.body:
A Chinese university with ties to the army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist.

Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense” group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website, the Reuters news agency reports.

The chips were bought for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record showed.

The Reuters investigation comes as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington, DC, over his lobbying for looser ⁠⁠restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

The H200 is among Nvidia’s most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical.

Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 ‌‌chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show.

Nvidia CEO Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve US technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on its technology.

However, some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips can speed China’s development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.

Based in the northwestern city of Xi’an, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites.

Washington’s Department of Commerce added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over the institute’s alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities, and its military research. Washington tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exporting controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances.

Northwestern Polytechnical’s purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them.

A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ⁠⁠that use such chips through domestic suppliers.

Several had close links to China’s defence industry or military research.

US President Donald Trump’s administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical.

Both Democrats and Republicans in the US Congress have urged stronger controls on China’s access to advanced AI ⁠⁠chips, such as chip-tracking requirements, and greater congressional oversight of exports.

This comes at a time of increased pressure on Nvidia’s Huang. Republican US Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to step down as CEO after his intimate relationship with Alice Huang, accused of working for Chinese intelligence, plunged the company into crisis.

“The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I ⁠⁠just think he’s got to go,” Cramer told Politico late on Tuesday.

Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with the alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

Jensen Huang – who cofounded Nvidia, the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple, more than three decades ago – admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife, but the company said it has no reason to believe US national security or confidential information has been compromised.

Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation on Sunday into whether the 63-year-old Taiwan-US dual national had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation after media reports linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based data centre company.
